code.title: INSERT and COMMIT: log first, fsync, flush later
code.python:
# INSERT + COMMIT: log first, fsync at commit, page flushed later
log_buffer, log_disk = [], []
page_ram, page_disk = {}, {}
lsn = 0

def insert(txn, key, val):
    global lsn
    lsn += 1
    log_buffer.append((lsn, txn, "INSERT", key, val))  # 1) log record first
    page_ram[key] = (val, lsn)                         # 2) page changed in RAM, pageLSN stamped

def commit(txn):
    global lsn
    lsn += 1
    log_buffer.append((lsn, txn, "COMMIT", None, None))
    log_disk.extend(log_buffer)   # 3) fsync of the log = the durability point
    log_buffer.clear()
    print("commit", txn, "acked; log records on disk:", len(log_disk))

def flush_page(key):
    val, page_lsn = page_ram[key]
    # WAL rule: the log up to pageLSN must already be on disk
    assert any(r[0] >= page_lsn for r in log_disk)
    page_disk[key] = val

insert("T1", "row1", "alice")
insert("T1", "row2", "bob")
commit("T1")
print("data pages on disk after commit:", page_disk)
# crash: RAM is lost, so redo from the durable log
recovered = {r[3]: r[4] for r in log_disk if r[2] == "INSERT"}
print("rebuilt from WAL after crash:", recovered)
flush_page("row1")  # background writer flushes later
print("data pages on disk after flush:", page_disk)

followUps: COMMIT returns before the WAL is flushed, so a crash can lose the last few acknowledged commits, but the database stays consistent. Postgres's WAL writer flushes in the background (within about 3 x wal_writer_delay, up to roughly 600 ms by default). Commit latency drops from one fsync (about 1 ms on SSD, 10 ms on spinning disk) to microseconds. It is not fsync = off, which can corrupt data. InnoDB's similar knob is innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit = 2.

The durability point is the fsync that makes the log record containing COMMIT reach stable storage. Before it, a crash rolls the transaction back; after it, redo guarantees the change survives. Flushing the data page is irrelevant to durability. Example: the commit record has LSN 120, the log is flushed up to 120, and only then does the client get OK. With group commit, 50 concurrent commits can share one fsync.

That is allowed (this is the STEAL policy) and is safe, because of the WAL rule: before the page goes to disk, the log up to its pageLSN is flushed first. If the server then crashes before COMMIT, recovery uses the logged undo information to remove the change (InnoDB undo log, ARIES undo). In Postgres the row version simply belongs to an aborted transaction and is invisible, so VACUUM cleans it later. The only cost is an extra write.

code.title: Slotted page: slots, holes and compaction

followUps: They are split off the page. Postgres uses TOAST: values above about 2 KB are compressed and, if still big, stored in chunks of about 2 KB in a side table, leaving a small pointer in the row. InnoDB (DYNAMIC format) moves long BLOB/TEXT/VARCHAR values to overflow pages and keeps a 20-byte pointer, and each 16 KB page must still hold at least 2 rows. The cost is extra I/O whenever the big column is read, so avoid SELECT * when you do not need it.

Fill factor is the percentage of each page that inserts may fill; the rest is kept free for later growth. Lower it (for example 70 to 90) on update-heavy tables so new row versions stay on the same page, which in Postgres allows cheap HOT updates without touching indexes. With fillfactor 80 on an 8 KB page, about 1.6 KB stays free. The price is a table about 25% bigger (1 / 0.8) and more pages to read. For append-only tables keep 100.

code.title: Buffer pool with pins and sequential flooding
code.python:
from collections import OrderedDict

class Pool:
    def __init__(self, n):
        self.n, self.frames = n, OrderedDict()   # page_id -> [pin, dirty]
        self.hits = self.misses = 0

    def fetch(self, p):
        if p in self.frames:
            self.hits += 1
            self.frames.move_to_end(p)           # most recently used
        else:
            self.misses += 1
            if len(self.frames) >= self.n:
                # victim = least recently used page that is NOT pinned
                v = next((k for k, f in self.frames.items() if f[0] == 0), None)
                if v is None:
                    raise RuntimeError("all pages pinned")
                if self.frames[v][1]:
                    print("  write back dirty page", v, "(log flushed first)")
                del self.frames[v]
            self.frames[p] = [0, False]
        self.frames[p][0] += 1                   # pin
        return p

    def unpin(self, p, dirty=False):
        self.frames[p][0] -= 1
        self.frames[p][1] |= dirty

pool = Pool(4)
for _ in range(3):                               # hot pages 1 and 2
    for p in (1, 2):
        pool.unpin(pool.fetch(p), dirty=(p == 1))
pool.fetch(99)                                   # stays pinned, can never be evicted
for p in range(10, 16):                          # one big sequential scan
    pool.unpin(pool.fetch(p))
print("resident after scan:", list(pool.frames))
print("hits", pool.hits, "misses", pool.misses)
print("hot page 2 resident:", 2 in pool.frames, "- plain LRU was flooded by the scan")

followUps: Because the database must control when a dirty page reaches disk, and the OS does not know about the WAL rule (log before page). With mmap the OS may write a dirty page at any moment, pages cannot be pinned, I/O stalls block threads invisibly, errors arrive as signals, and TLB shootdowns slow multicore scans. The OS also uses a generic policy that big scans flood. InnoDB bypasses the OS cache with O_DIRECT; Postgres still double-buffers through it.

InnoDB reads with O_DIRECT, so the buffer pool is the only cache: on a dedicated server give it 50 to 75% of RAM (for 64 GB, about 40 to 48 GB). Postgres also benefits from the OS cache, so shared_buffers is usually about 25% (16 GB of 64 GB), and effective_cache_size tells the planner about the rest. Check that the hit ratio stays above about 99% for OLTP, and leave RAM for connections, sorts and the OS.

A latch is a short internal mutex or reader-writer lock protecting a page's in-memory structure; it is held for microseconds, has no deadlock detection and is released as soon as the page operation ends. A lock is a logical, transaction-level lock on a row or table, held until commit or rollback, with a wait graph and deadlock detection. Example: a B-tree split latches parent and child briefly; SELECT ... FOR UPDATE keeps a row lock for the whole transaction.

code.title: STEAL and NO-FORCE with undo and redo
code.python:
# STEAL + NO-FORCE: uncommitted data may reach disk, committed data may not
disk = {"A": 0, "B": 0}
ram = {"A": 0, "B": 0}
log = []                       # (txn, page, before, after) - already durable

def update(t, k, new):
    log.append((t, k, ram[k], new))   # before-image (undo) and after-image (redo)
    ram[k] = new

update("T1", "A", 5)           # T1 never commits
disk["A"] = ram["A"]           # STEAL: page written early; the log is on disk first
update("T2", "B", 7)
committed = {"T2"}             # NO-FORCE: B is not written at commit
print("before crash  disk:", disk, "committed:", sorted(committed))
# crash: RAM lost. recovery:
for t, k, before, after in log:            # redo committed work
    if t in committed:
        disk[k] = after
for t, k, before, after in reversed(log):  # undo uncommitted work
    if t not in committed:
        disk[k] = before
print("after recovery disk:", disk)

followUps: Postgres is effectively STEAL plus NO-FORCE, but without undo records. Dirty pages with uncommitted rows may be written (STEAL) and commit does not force data pages (NO-FORCE), so the WAL only needs redo. Undo is unnecessary because MVCC keeps row versions tagged with the writer's transaction id; an aborted writer's versions are invisible and VACUUM removes them later. InnoDB, in contrast, keeps a separate undo log.

Then a commit can be acknowledged while its log records still sit in a volatile cache, so a power loss silently loses committed transactions. Worse, a data page can reach the platter before its log record, which breaks the WAL rule and makes recovery wrong or impossible, and the database cannot easily detect this. Fixes: disks with power-loss-protected caches, turning off volatile write caches, and testing with pg_test_fsync. Postgres now PANICs on fsync errors instead of retrying.

code.title: ARIES analysis, redo and undo on the example log
code.python:
# Log: (lsn, txn, page, old, new) or (lsn, txn, "COMMIT")
log = [(1, "T1", "A", 0, 5), (2, "T2", "B", 0, 7), (3, "T1", "COMMIT"),
       (4, "T2", "C", 0, 9), (5, "T3", "A", 5, 8), (6, "T3", "COMMIT")]
disk = {"A": (0, 0), "B": (7, 2), "C": (0, 0)}   # page -> (value, pageLSN)
# Analysis: who committed?
winners = {r[1] for r in log if r[2] == "COMMIT"}
losers = {r[1] for r in log} - winners
print("winners", sorted(winners), "losers", sorted(losers))
# Redo: repeat history, even for losers, if pageLSN < lsn
for r in log:
    if r[2] != "COMMIT":
        lsn, t, page, old, new = r
        if disk[page][1] < lsn:
            disk[page] = (new, lsn)
            print("redo lsn", lsn, page, "=", new)
        else:
            print("skip lsn", lsn, "page already has it")
# Undo: roll back losers newest first, writing CLRs
clr = 7
for r in reversed(log):
    if r[1] in losers and r[2] != "COMMIT":
        lsn, t, page, old, new = r
        disk[page] = (old, clr)
        print("undo lsn", lsn, page, "<-", old, "CLR", clr)
        clr += 1
print("final:", {k: v[0] for k, v in disk.items()})

followUps: Because redo must rebuild the exact page state at the crash, so that the pageLSN test and the undo records (which may assume earlier changes, slot moves or splits) are valid. Skipping losers would leave pages in a state that no log record describes. It also supports row-level locking, where a loser and a winner changed the same page. In the example, redoing T2's update C = 9 (LSN 4) is wasted, but undo then writes a CLR to remove it correctly.

A fuzzy checkpoint writes a begin record, then an end record containing a snapshot of the dirty page table (page and recLSN) and the active transaction table, without stopping writers or flushing the dirty pages. It is fuzzy because transactions keep running while the tables are copied, so the snapshot is not an exact instant. Analysis scans forward from the begin record to correct it. Example: dirty table {A: 1, C: 4}, so redo starts at the minimum recLSN, 1.

Recovery time is bounded by the log from the oldest recLSN in the dirty page table to the end, plus the undo work of loser transactions. Checkpoint frequency and dirty-page flushing keep this short. Example: 2 GB of log at 200 MB/s of replay is about 10 seconds; cold-cache random page reads make it slower. A huge uncommitted transaction adds undo time, often as long as the work itself.

code.title: Write amplification: B-tree pages vs LSM runs
code.python:
import random
random.seed(1)
N, ROW, PAGE, PER = 20000, 100, 4096, 40       # 40 rows per page -> 500 pages
keys = [random.randrange(N) for _ in range(N)]  # random update keys
useful = N * ROW

# B-tree: each batch of 1000 updates rewrites every dirty page once
btree = 0
for i in range(0, N, 1000):
    dirty_pages = {k // PER for k in keys[i:i + 1000]}
    btree += len(dirty_pages) * PAGE

# LSM: sequential flushes of 1000 rows; merge 4 equal runs into one
runs, lsm = [], 0
for i in range(0, N, 1000):
    runs.append(1000)
    lsm += 1000 * ROW                           # flush
    while len(runs) >= 4 and runs[-4:] == [runs[-1]] * 4:
        merged = sum(runs[-4:])
        del runs[-4:]
        runs.append(merged)
        lsm += merged * ROW                     # compaction rewrite
print("logical data written:", useful, "bytes")
print("B-tree bytes written:", btree, "amplification", round(btree / useful, 1))
print("LSM    bytes written:", lsm, "amplification", round(lsm / useful, 1))

followUps: The RUM conjecture says an access method cannot be optimal at Read cost, Update cost and Memory (space) overhead at once: improving two worsens the third. A B-tree favors reads; an LSM favors updates and space but pays more on reads; a Bloom filter buys cheaper reads for extra memory. Example: 10 bits per key of Bloom filter (about 1.25 bytes/key) cuts most useless run lookups, but a 1 billion key store then needs about 1.25 GB of RAM for it.

A range delete is one range tombstone (start, end, sequence) that hides older keys on reads and disappears when compaction reaches the bottom, instead of millions of point tombstones. Secondary indexes are just more key spaces: key = (indexed value, primary key), one extra write per index per row. A non-unique index insert is a blind write; a unique index needs a read first, and updating an indexed column must delete the old entry, which needs a read of the old row.

The Bε-tree (TokuDB, fractal tree) keeps a message buffer in each internal node and pushes batched writes down to children, so inserts cost far fewer I/Os than in a B-tree while reads stay tree-like. The Bw-tree (Hekaton, Azure Cosmos DB) is latch-free: it chains delta records off a mapping table and uses a log-structured store. Other hybrids exist, but these two are the usual answers.

code.title: Leveled vs size-tiered write amplification
code.python:
import math
T, LEVELS = 10, 5                  # size ratio and number of levels
FLUSH_MB, DATA_MB = 64, 1_000_000  # memtable flush size, total data (1 TB)

# Leveled: a byte is merged ~T/2 times on average at each level
leveled = 1 + 1 + LEVELS * T / 2   # WAL + flush + per-level merges
# Size-tiered: a byte is rewritten once per tier, tiers = log_T(N / flush)
tiers = math.ceil(math.log(DATA_MB / FLUSH_MB, T))
tiered = 1 + 1 + tiers
print("leveled: T =", T, "levels =", LEVELS, "-> WA about", leveled,
      "(worst case", 2 + T * LEVELS, ") space amp about", round(1 + 1 / T, 2), "x")
print("tiered : tiers =", tiers, "-> WA about", tiered,
      "read up to", T - 1, "runs per tier, space amp up to 2x")
ingest = 50
print("ingest", ingest, "MB/s with WA 22 needs", ingest * 22, "MB/s of disk writes")

followUps: It sizes the levels from the bottom up instead of from L1 down, so the last level holds about 90% of the data and each level above is 1/T of the one below. That bounds space amplification near 1 + 1/T even when the database is smaller than the configured target. Example: 100 GB of data with T = 10 gives levels of about 100, 10, 1 and 0.1 GB, a total near 111 GB, so 1.11x.

Disk writes needed are ingest x WA = 50 x 22 = 1,100 MB/s, about 95 TB per day, and compaction also reads about as much, so plan for roughly 1.1 GB/s of writes plus 1 GB/s of reads sustained, ideally with 2x headroom so compaction never falls behind. One fast NVMe drive (2 to 3 GB/s) is borderline; a SATA SSD (about 500 MB/s) is far too slow, so you need several drives or sharding. Also check flash endurance.

diskWrite = ingest * WA;   // 50 * 22 = 1100 MB/s
diskRead  = ingest * WA;   // approx, compaction inputs
need = 2 * max(diskWrite, diskRead);  // headroom

code.title: Mini LSM key-value engine
code.python:
class MiniLSM:
    def __init__(self, limit=3):
        self.wal, self.mem, self.sst, self.limit = [], {}, [], limit  # sst: newest first

    def put(self, k, v):
        self.wal.append((k, v))            # 1) durable log first
        self.mem[k] = v                    # 2) memtable
        if len(self.mem) >= self.limit:    # 3) flush full memtable as sorted, immutable run
            self.sst.insert(0, dict(sorted(self.mem.items())))
            self.mem, self.wal = {}, []    # WAL segment can be deleted
            print("  flushed ->", self.sst[0])

    def delete(self, k):
        self.put(k, None)                  # tombstone

    def get(self, k):
        for level in [self.mem] + self.sst:  # newest data wins
            if k in level:
                return level[k]
        return None

    def compact(self):
        merged = {}
        for run in reversed(self.sst):     # oldest first, newer overwrites
            merged.update(run)
        self.sst = [{k: v for k, v in merged.items() if v is not None}]  # drop tombstones
        print("  compacted ->", self.sst[0])

db = MiniLSM()
for k, v in [("a", 1), ("b", 2), ("c", 3), ("a", 10), ("d", 4)]:
    db.put(k, v)
db.delete("b")
db.put("e", 5)
print("get a:", db.get("a"), "get b:", db.get("b"), "get d:", db.get("d"))
print("recover memtable from WAL:", dict(db.wal))
db.compact()
print("runs left:", len(db.sst), "get c:", db.get("c"))

followUps: Stalls happen when L0 files or pending compaction bytes pile up faster than compaction drains them. Absorb bursts with 3 to 4 memtables, give L0 to L1 compaction priority and subcompactions, set a slowdown trigger (for example 20 L0 files) that gradually delays writes before the hard stop trigger (36), smooth compaction I/O with a rate limiter, and apply backpressure or queueing at the client. Most important: provision bandwidth for ingest x WA, with headroom.

Give each write batch one sequence number and one WAL record so it is atomic. Reads take a snapshot at a sequence number and ignore newer versions. For isolation, either use optimistic transactions (at commit, abort if any key read or written has a version newer than the snapshot) or pessimistic row locks in a lock table. For distributed commit add a prepare record to the WAL (two-phase commit). RocksDB's TransactionDB works this way.

In the MANIFEST: an append-only log of version edits (add file 42 at level 2, delete files 17 and 18), fsynced for each edit. A small CURRENT file names the active manifest. To rotate, write a fresh snapshot to a temp file, fsync it, then atomically rename it over CURRENT and fsync the directory. SST files are fully written and fsynced before the edit that references them is logged; files nobody references are deleted at recovery.

Keep InnoDB for read-heavy OLTP with tight p99 latency, many secondary indexes, frequent small in-place updates, applications that depend on gap locks and REPEATABLE READ behavior, and teams that need mature tooling such as online DDL and backups. It also fits when data is small enough that space does not matter. Example: a 200 GB orders table on plenty of SSD. MyRocks pays off mainly when the data is large and write- or space-bound.

Each index is a separate key space in RocksDB: key = (index id, indexed columns, primary key), with an empty or covering value. A non-unique insert is a blind write with no read. A unique index first does a point lookup to check duplicates. Updating an indexed column writes a tombstone for the old entry plus a new entry. A lookup through a secondary index needs a second get on the primary key unless the index covers the query.

code.title: Random vs ordered keys in a clustered B-tree
code.python:
import bisect, random
CAP = 100                      # keys per leaf page
rng = random.Random(1)

def build(keys):
    leaves = [[]]              # each leaf is a sorted list; leaves kept in key order
    firsts = [0]               # smallest key bound of each leaf
    splits = 0
    for k in keys:
        i = bisect.bisect_right(firsts, k) - 1
        leaf = leaves[i]
        bisect.insort(leaf, k)
        if len(leaf) > CAP:
            splits += 1
            if leaf[-1] == k:                  # insert at the right edge: start a fresh page
                new = [leaf.pop()]
            else:                              # middle insert: 50/50 split
                half = len(leaf) // 2
                new, leaf[half:] = leaf[half:], []
            leaves.insert(i + 1, new)
            firsts.insert(i + 1, new[0])
    return len(leaves), splits, sum(map(len, leaves)) / (len(leaves) * CAP)

N = 20000
ordered = list(range(N))                       # AUTO_INCREMENT / UUIDv7-like
shuffled = ordered[:]
rng.shuffle(shuffled)                          # UUIDv4-like
for name, keys in (("ordered", ordered), ("random ", shuffled)):
    pages, splits, fill = build(keys)
    print(name, "pages:", pages, "splits:", splits, "avg fill: %d%%" % round(fill * 100))

followUps: The Postgres heap is not sorted by primary key, so random UUIDs do not fragment the table: new rows go to any page with free space. The primary-key B-tree is still hit at random leaves, with 50/50 splits (about 70% full), poor cache locality, and a full-page image in the WAL for each leaf touched after a checkpoint. So the damage is smaller than in InnoDB's clustered case, but UUIDv7 still makes the index and WAL much smaller.

Add a new key column (BIGINT or UUIDv7), backfill it in batches of about 10k rows ordered by created_at with throttling, and dual-write new rows with the app or a trigger. Build the new unique index online (CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, gh-ost, pt-online-schema-change), migrate the foreign keys, switch reads behind a flag, then rename and drop the old key. Keep the old UUID as a unique column if outside systems use it. Copying 2 TB at 100 MB/s alone takes about 5.6 hours.

code.title: Column store: RLE, zone maps, column pruning
code.python:
# 1000 rows: (country, amount). Row store vs column store ideas
countries = ["DE"] * 400 + ["FR"] * 300 + ["US"] * 300          # sorted column
amounts = [(i * 37) % 1000 for i in range(1000)]
print("first rows:", list(zip(countries, amounts))[:3])

# 1) RLE compression on the sorted column
rle, prev = [], None
for c in countries:
    if c == prev:
        rle[-1][1] += 1
    else:
        rle.append([c, 1])
        prev = c
print("RLE:", rle, "-> 3 pairs instead of 1000 values")

# 2) zone maps: min/max per block of 100 values lets us skip blocks
BLOCK = 100
zones = [(min(amounts[i:i + BLOCK]), max(amounts[i:i + BLOCK]))
         for i in range(0, 1000, BLOCK)]
want = 995                                  # query: amount >= 995
scanned = [z for z in zones if z[1] >= want]
print("blocks:", len(zones), "scanned:", len(scanned))

# 3) read only the needed column, aggregate on it
total = sum(a for a in amounts if a >= want)
print("sum(amount) where amount >= 995 =", total, "(only 1 of 2 columns read)")

followUps: MergeTree writes each insert as a small immutable part sorted by the primary key, and background merges combine parts into bigger sorted ones, just as LSM compaction does. Its primary index is sparse (one mark per 8,192 rows). Differences: there is no memtable or WAL by default, so every insert becomes a part and clients must batch thousands of rows, there are no levels, and updates are mutations that rewrite whole parts.

Parquet is an on-disk columnar file format: compressed, encoded, split into row groups with min/max statistics. Arrow is an in-memory columnar format: uncompressed, aligned buffers made for fast computation and zero-copy exchange between systems. Typical flow: read Parquet, decode into Arrow arrays, compute. Example: one million int32 values are exactly 4 MB in Arrow, but a few hundred KB or less in Parquet if dictionary or RLE encoding applies.

HTAP makes sense when analytics needs very fresh data (seconds old) and the analytical load is moderate, so one system saves you an ETL pipeline. Examples: fraud checks on live orders, dashboards over the last hour. Typical design: a row store for transactions plus a column replica (TiDB with TiFlash, SingleStore, SQL Server columnstore). It does not make sense when heavy scans would hurt OLTP latency or data is huge; a separate warehouse is better.

code.title: Torn page detected by checksum, fixed by doublewrite
code.python:
import zlib
HALF = 8                       # pretend the disk writes 8 bytes atomically
old = b"OLD-DATA" * 2          # 16-byte "page" on disk
new = b"NEWER-DT" * 2

def with_crc(page):
    return page + zlib.crc32(page).to_bytes(4, "big")

def ok(blob):
    return zlib.crc32(blob[:-4]) == int.from_bytes(blob[-4:], "big")

disk = with_crc(old)
doublewrite = with_crc(new)    # 1) page first written to the doublewrite area, fsynced
# 2) crash while writing in place: first half new, second half old
torn = new[:HALF] + old[HALF:]
disk = with_crc(torn)[:-4] + disk[-4:]    # checksum still belongs to the old page
print("in-place page:", disk[:-4], "checksum valid:", ok(disk))
if not ok(disk):                          # recovery: restore from the doublewrite copy
    disk = doublewrite
print("after recovery:", disk[:-4], "checksum valid:", ok(disk))
# Postgres alternative: full_page_writes puts the whole image in the WAL

followUps: Because the first change to a page after each checkpoint writes the whole 8 KB image into the WAL instead of a small delta, and right after a checkpoint almost every modified page is on its first touch. A 100-byte change then costs about 8 KB, roughly 80x. Example: 10,000 random row updates just after a checkpoint log about 80 MB instead of 1 MB. The rate decays as pages are already covered, giving a sawtooth. Longer checkpoint intervals and wal_compression reduce it.

A checksum is computed when a page is written and verified when it is read, so bit rot or a bad sector that appeared after the write shows up as a mismatch instead of silently wrong data. A replica has its own storage, so a mismatch there means that replica's disk is damaged while the primary's copy may be fine; you can rebuild the replica. Periodic scans (pg_checksums, scrub jobs) find rot before it reaches backups. It cannot catch corruption in RAM before the write.

code.title: Crash recovery time from WAL volume
code.python:
# Crash recovery time ~ WAL to replay / replay speed
def recovery(wal_gb_since_oldest_dirty, replay_mb_s, undo_s=0):
    return wal_gb_since_oldest_dirty * 1024 / replay_mb_s + undo_s

cases = [
    ("big redo capacity, cold cache", 40, 30, 60),
    ("smaller checkpoints", 4, 30, 60),
    ("small checkpoints + prefetch", 4, 120, 60),
    ("small checkpoints + prefetch, no giant txn", 4, 120, 5),
]
for name, gb, speed, undo in cases:
    secs = recovery(gb, speed, undo)
    print(name + ":", gb, "GB at", speed, "MB/s +", undo, "s undo =",
          round(secs / 60, 1), "min")
print("hot standby failover: about 0.2 min")

followUps: More frequent checkpoints shorten recovery because less WAL has to be replayed, but cost more I/O: dirty pages are flushed more often and more first-touch full-page images are written to the WAL, which raises write amplification. Example: checkpoint_timeout of 5 minutes means up to about 5 minutes of WAL to replay; 30 minutes means up to 30, but far fewer full-page writes. Set checkpoint_completion_target near 0.9 to spread the writes.

After a crash InnoDB opens the database and rolls back unfinished transactions in the background, holding their row locks until the undo is done. Rollback is row by row and often as slow as, or slower than, the original work, so a transaction that changed 50 million rows can keep those rows locked for a long time after restart. Avoid it by running big updates in batches of about 10k rows with a commit each. You can see the risk in information_schema.innodb_trx.trx_rows_modified.

code.title: Tombstones slow range scans until compaction
code.python:
old_run = {"k%03d" % i: "v" for i in range(200)}               # older, bigger run
new_run = {"k%03d" % i: None for i in range(0, 195)}           # tombstones (None)
new_run.update({"k%03d" % i: "live" for i in range(195, 200)})  # 5 live rows

def scan(runs, lo, hi):
    seen, tomb = {}, 0
    for run in runs:                      # newest run first
        for k, v in run.items():
            if lo <= k <= hi and k not in seen:
                seen[k] = v
                if v is None:
                    tomb += 1             # scan must step over each tombstone
    live = {k: v for k, v in seen.items() if v is not None}
    return len(live), tomb

print("before compaction runs: 2, entries:", len(old_run) + len(new_run))
print("scan k000..k199 -> (live rows, tombstones stepped over):",
      scan([new_run, old_run], "k000", "k199"))

# compaction into the bottom level: newest wins, tombstones are dropped
merged = dict(old_run)
merged.update(new_run)
bottom = {k: v for k, v in merged.items() if v is not None}
print("after compaction entries:", len(bottom))
print("scan again ->", scan([bottom], "k000", "k199"))

followUps: A snapshot or open iterator reads the database as of a sequence number, so compaction may not drop any version or tombstone that this snapshot could still need. Example: a snapshot at sequence 100 is held for hours; a key deleted at sequence 150 still keeps its old value from sequence 90 on disk, and the files that hold it. Fix: keep snapshots and long scans short, and watch for old snapshots in metrics.

With leveled compaction a tombstone is pushed down level by level and space returns steadily, with space amplification near 1.1x. With tiered compaction dead data stays until its tier merges, so space amplification can reach 2x or more, tombstones hang around until a big merge, and reads check more runs and skip more tombstones per scan. TTL or time-window compaction avoids this by dropping whole files in either strategy.
